moduleTitle: Incarnation: Jesus as the incarnate Son and divine Word, fully God and fully human

note.specFocus: AQA 8062 Catholic Christianity, key beliefs: the Incarnation – Jesus as incarnate Son and divine Word, fully God and fully human; the scriptural basis for this belief (including John 1 and the infancy narratives).
note.summary:
KEY IDEA: The Incarnation (Latin in carne, "in flesh") is the belief that God the Son, the second person of the Trinity, became a human being in Jesus of Nazareth. He did this without ceasing to be God. Jesus is therefore one divine person with two natures: fully God and fully human (CCC 464–469). The Nicene Creed says he "came down from heaven, and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man".

THE DIVINE WORD (John 1): John's Gospel begins: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God" (John 1:1). "Word" is the Greek Logos, God's eternal self-expression and reason, through whom "all things came into being" (1:3). Then: "the Word became flesh and lived among us… full of grace and truth" (John 1:14). The Son existed before he was born as Jesus. The Incarnation is God personally entering human history.

SCRIPTURAL BASIS FOR THE INCARNATION AND VIRGIN BIRTH:
• Matthew 1:18–25: Mary is found to be with child "from the Holy Spirit". The angel tells Joseph to name him Jesus, "for he will save his people from their sins". Matthew links this to Isaiah 7:14: "they shall name him Emmanuel… God is with us".
• Luke 1:26–38 (the Annunciation): Gabriel tells Mary she will conceive. "The Holy Spirit will come upon you… the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God" (1:35). Mary replies, "Here am I, the servant of the Lord" (1:38).
• Philippians 2:6–8: Christ "emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being born in human likeness".
• Colossians 1:15: Christ is "the image of the invisible God".

FULLY HUMAN: Jesus was born, grew, ate, felt tired, wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35), was tempted (Matthew 4), felt anguish in Gethsemane and truly died. He had a human mind and will. He was like us "in every respect… yet without sin" (Hebrews 4:15).

FULLY DIVINE: Jesus forgave sins (Mark 2:5–12), worked miracles, accepted worship, called God "Abba", rose from the dead, and said "The Father and I are one" (John 10:30). Thomas calls him "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28).

CHURCH TEACHING: Early heresies denied one side or the other. Docetism said Jesus only seemed human. Arianism said he was not truly God. The Council of Nicaea (325) affirmed his divinity. The Council of Chalcedon (451) declared Christ is one person "in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation". Mary is honoured as Theotokos, "Mother of God" (Council of Ephesus, 431), because the one she bore is God (CCC 495). Christmas (25 December) and the Feast of the Annunciation (25 March) celebrate the Incarnation. At the Creed's words "and by the Holy Spirit was incarnate…" Catholics bow.

WHY IT MATTERS:
• Revelation: in Jesus, God is shown fully. "Whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9).
• Salvation: only one who is both God and human can reconcile humanity with God (CCC 457–460). "The Word became flesh… to save us by reconciling us with God."
• Example: Jesus is a model of holiness. The Incarnation also makes human life and the material world holy, which underpins the sacraments and the dignity of every person.
• God with us: God understands human suffering from the inside.

DIFFERENT VIEWS: Most Christians accept Chalcedon. Some liberal Christians see the virgin birth as symbolic and stress Jesus's humanity as a uniquely God-filled teacher. Jews regard Jesus as a teacher but not the Messiah or divine. Muslims honour Isa (Jesus) as a great prophet born of a virgin but reject that he is God or God's Son.

KEY TERMS: Incarnation, Logos/Word, Emmanuel, Annunciation, virgin birth, two natures, hypostatic union, Theotokos, Chalcedon, docetism.

questions.question:
Which one of the following phrases from John's Gospel refers to the Incarnation?
A) 'I am the bread of life'
B) 'The Word became flesh and lived among us'
C) 'It is finished'
D) 'Peace be with you'
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: B) 'The Word became flesh and lived among us' (John 1:14).

This verse describes the eternal Word (the Son) taking human nature. A is an 'I am' saying about the Eucharist (John 6:35). C is Jesus's last word on the cross (John 19:30). D is the risen Jesus's greeting (John 20:19).
questions.examTip: Learn John 1:1 and 1:14 word-for-word. They are the key texts for the Incarnation.

questions.question:
Which title, confirmed at the Council of Ephesus, means Mary is the 'God-bearer' or 'Mother of God'?
A) Messiah
B) Logos
C) Theotokos
D) Paraclete
questions.modelAnswer:
Answer: C) Theotokos.

Theotokos ('God-bearer') was affirmed at Ephesus in 431 because the child Mary bore is the divine Son. Messiah means 'anointed one' (Jesus). Logos means 'Word' (the Son). Paraclete means 'Advocate' (the Holy Spirit).
questions.examTip: Titles of Mary are about who Jesus is. Theotokos protects the belief that Jesus is truly God.

questions.question: Give one piece of evidence from the Gospels that Jesus was fully human.
questions.modelAnswer:
Any one from:
• He was born as a baby to Mary (Luke 2:7)
• He wept at Lazarus's tomb (John 11:35)
• He was hungry after fasting / tempted in the desert (Matthew 4:2)
• He felt anguish and sweated in Gethsemane (Luke 22:44)
• He was thirsty and died on the cross (John 19:28–30)
questions.examTip: Pick one clear example. A Bible reference makes the answer stronger, but it is not required for 1 mark.

questions.question: Give one meaning of the name 'Emmanuel'.
questions.modelAnswer: God is with us (Matthew 1:23, quoting Isaiah 7:14).
questions.examTip: Short 'Give' answers only need the meaning. 'God with us' is enough.

questions.question: Explain two ways in which belief in the Incarnation influences Catholics today.
questions.modelAnswer:
First way: Catholics celebrate the Incarnation in worship (1 mark). At Christmas they attend Midnight Mass and set up cribs (nativity scenes), a custom linked to St Francis of Assisi. During the Creed they bow at the words 'by the Holy Spirit was incarnate of the Virgin Mary, and became man', showing reverence for God becoming human (2nd mark).

Second way: Because God became human, Catholics believe human life and the physical world are holy (1 mark). Jesus shared ordinary human life, so Catholics believe God can be met in other people, especially the poor (Matthew 25:40). This inspires charity work and respect for the dignity of every human being (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Use real practices (bowing in the Creed, Christmas, the Angelus) to show influence.

questions.question: Explain two different Christian beliefs about the nature of Jesus.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: Catholics, along with Orthodox and most Protestant Christians, believe Jesus is one person who is fully God and fully human (1 mark). The Council of Chalcedon (451) taught that his two natures are united 'without confusion, change, division or separation', so Jesus could both suffer as a human and save as God (2nd mark).

Second, different belief: Some liberal Christians emphasise Jesus's humanity (1 mark). They see him as a man uniquely open to God, and see stories such as the virgin birth as symbolic expressions of his importance rather than literal biology. For them, Jesus's moral teaching and example matter more than metaphysical claims about divinity (2nd mark).
questions.examTip: Two genuinely different views are needed. One traditional and one liberal view is a safe pairing.

questions.question:
Explain two Catholic beliefs about the Incarnation.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First belief: Jesus is the eternal Son of God who took on human nature (1 mark). He did not begin to exist at his birth. As the second person of the Trinity he existed from eternity and 'came down from heaven', as the Nicene Creed says, becoming man without ceasing to be God (2nd mark).

Second belief: Jesus was conceived by the power of the Holy Spirit and born of the Virgin Mary (1 mark). The angel tells Mary, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you… the child to be born will be holy; he will be called Son of God' (Luke 1:35). This shows his conception was a unique act of God (2nd mark).

Source of authority: John 1:1 says 'the Word was God', and 1:14 says 'the Word became flesh and lived among us'. Together these verses show that the divine Word, who was God, truly became human. That is the core of the Catholic belief that Jesus is fully God and fully human (2 marks).
questions.examTip: Two distinct beliefs, for example 'eternal Son becomes human' and 'virgin birth', are safer than two versions of the same idea.

questions.question:
Explain two reasons why the Incarnation is important for Catholics.
Refer to sacred writings or another source of Christian belief and teaching in your answer.
questions.modelAnswer:
First reason: The Incarnation makes salvation possible (1 mark). Catholics believe only someone who is both God and human could restore the broken relationship between God and humanity. As a human, Jesus could offer his life on our behalf. As God, his sacrifice has infinite value (CCC 457) (2nd mark).

Second reason: In Jesus, God reveals himself fully and personally (1 mark). People no longer have to guess what God is like. They see God's love in Jesus's words, healing and forgiveness, and he is a perfect model of how to live (2nd mark).

Source of authority: Jesus says to Philip, 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). Through the Incarnation, God the Father can be known by looking at Jesus. This supports the belief that the Incarnation is God's fullest revelation of himself (2 marks).
evidence: Matthew 1:21 'he will save his people from their sins'
questions.examTip: 'Why important' questions need reasons, not just a description. Start each point with 'because…'.

questions.question:
'Jesus was just a good man.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Most historians agree that Jesus was a real Jewish teacher who lived in first-century Palestine and was crucified under Pontius Pilate. His teaching, such as 'love your enemies' (Matthew 5:44) and the parable of the Good Samaritan, is admired by people of all faiths and none. A humanist may accept that Jesus was an outstanding moral example while seeing claims about divinity as later additions by his followers. Such claims cannot be scientifically proven.

Other religions also honour Jesus without calling him God. Judaism sees him as a teacher but not the Messiah. Islam reveres Isa as a great prophet born of a virgin, but teaches that God has no son. Some liberal Christians focus on Jesus's humanity and see the miracle stories and virgin birth as symbolic.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

Catholic teaching firmly rejects the idea that Jesus was only a good man. The Nicene Creed calls him 'true God from true God… consubstantial with the Father'. The Church teaches the Incarnation: the eternal Word 'became flesh' (John 1:14) in Jesus, who is fully God and fully human (Council of Chalcedon, 451; CCC 464).

The Gospels present Jesus doing things only God can do. He forgives sins, and the onlookers ask, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' (Mark 2:7). He calms storms, raises the dead and rises from the dead himself. He says 'The Father and I are one' (John 10:30), and Thomas worships him as 'My Lord and my God!' (John 20:28).

C. S. Lewis's well-known argument (the 'trilemma') says that someone who claimed to be God cannot be 'just a good man'. Either he was lying (bad), deluded (mad), or telling the truth (God). On this view, 'just a good man' is the one option that does not fit the evidence of his claims.

The resurrection is central here. St Paul writes that 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith has been in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:17). The rapid growth of the early Church, and apostles willing to die for their belief, suggest that they experienced something more than a good man's death.

CONCLUSION

The statement is reasonable from a non-religious or non-Christian point of view, which accepts Jesus's goodness but not his divinity. But for Catholics it misses what the Gospels and the Church actually claim. Jesus's authority to forgive sins, his resurrection and the Church's consistent teaching from Nicaea to today point to the belief that he is God incarnate. Since the 'good man' view ignores Jesus's own claims about himself, the stronger argument is that he was more than a good man, though this remains a matter of faith rather than proof.
questions.examTip: Including non-religious and other-faith views strengthens a 12-mark answer, but make sure Catholic teaching is clearly explained.

questions.question:
'The Incarnation is the most important Catholic belief.'
Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• refer to Catholic teaching
• reach a justified conclusion.
questions.modelAnswer:
ARGUMENTS IN SUPPORT

Without the Incarnation, almost every other Christian belief would collapse. If the Word had not 'become flesh' (John 1:14), there would be no life of Jesus, no crucifixion, no resurrection and no Eucharist. Salvation depends on Jesus being both God and man. As man he could offer himself for humanity, and as God his sacrifice could reconcile the whole world with God (CCC 457). In this sense the Incarnation is the foundation on which the rest is built.

The Incarnation also reveals who God is. Jesus said, 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). In the Incarnation, the God who is beyond all things becomes Emmanuel, 'God with us' (Matthew 1:23). It also explains why Catholics treat physical things such as bread, wine, water and oil as channels of grace in the sacraments. Because God took flesh, matter can carry the divine.

ARGUMENTS AGAINST

The Catechism calls the Trinity 'the central mystery of Christian faith and life… the source of all the other mysteries' (CCC 234). Without the Trinity there would be no eternal Son to become incarnate. Many Catholics would therefore say the Trinity is the more fundamental belief.

Others would point to the resurrection. St Paul wrote, 'If Christ has not been raised, your faith has been in vain' (1 Corinthians 15:17). The Church calls Easter the 'feast of feasts' and celebrates it every Sunday. It is the resurrection that proves Jesus's victory over sin and death and gives Catholics hope of eternal life.

In practical terms, many Catholics might say the Eucharist matters most, because it is 'the source and summit of the Christian life' (Lumen Gentium 11; CCC 1324). It is how they meet Christ each week. Some theologians also argue that it is unhelpful to rank beliefs at all. Catholic doctrines form a connected whole (the 'hierarchy of truths' links each truth to the central mystery of Christ).

CONCLUSION

The Incarnation is clearly essential. Salvation, revelation and the sacramental life all depend on it. However, calling it the most important belief is hard to justify when the Church itself names the Trinity as the central mystery and the resurrection as the high point of the liturgical year. The most convincing conclusion is that the Incarnation is one of a few core beliefs, alongside the Trinity and the resurrection, that cannot be separated. Each makes sense only in the light of the others.
questions.examTip: When asked whether something is 'most important', compare it with named alternatives (here the Trinity, the resurrection and the Eucharist) and give reasons for each.
